documents.text: Welcome to CS229. Today we begin optimization fundamentals. In supervised learning, our objective is to minimize an empirical risk or loss function J of theta over our dataset of examples.

The gradient vector nabla J(theta) points in the direction of greatest rate of increase of the loss. Consequently, to minimize loss, we take steps in the opposite direction: theta equals theta minus alpha times nabla J(theta).
Let us examine the learning rate alpha. If alpha is chosen too small, gradient descent will be excruciatingly slow, requiring millions of epochs to reach the bowl of the loss surface.
Conversely, if alpha is set too large, gradient descent can overshoot the global minimum, bounce across ravine walls, and catastrophically diverge towards numerical infinity.

To address oscillations in ill-conditioned ravines, we introduce the Momentum optimizer. Momentum accumulates an exponential moving average of past gradients, dampening perpendicular oscillations while accelerating along the consistent downhill trajectory.

Chapter 4: Numerical Computation. Most deep learning algorithms involve continuous optimization. Gradient descent is an iterative first-order optimization algorithm for finding a local minimum of a differentiable function. The step size is governed by hyperparameter alpha, commonly designated the learning rate.

Chapter 6: Deep Feedforward Networks and Backpropagation. Backpropagation applies the multivariable calculus chain rule backward from the output layer to calculate partial derivatives of the scalar loss with respect to all internal weight tensors W and bias vectors b.

Chapter 8: Optimization for Training Deep Models. In Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), instead of computing the true expectation of the gradient over the entire training set of size N, we compute an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate using a mini-batch of size m (typically 32 to 256).

Slide 2: The Optimization Landscape. Loss surfaces in deep networks are non-convex, characterized by vast plateaus, saddle points with high condition numbers, and ravines. Saddle points are far more prevalent than true local minima in high-dimensional parameter spaces.

Slide 5: Adaptive Learning Rate Algorithms: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation). Adam combines the advantages of Momentum (first moment estimate) and RMSProp (uncentered second moment estimate) with bias-correction terms to handle sparse gradients naturally.
Gradient Descent: Parameter update rule theta = theta - alpha * grad(J). If alpha is too large, it diverges.

Object-Oriented Programming
• Object-oriented programming (OOP) is at the core of Java. In fact, all 
Java programs are to at least some extent object-oriented. 
Two Paradigms: All computer programs consist of two elements: code
and data. A program can be conceptually organised around its code or
around its data. That is, some programs are written around “what is
happening” and others are written around “who is being affected.”

• An essential element of object-oriented programming is abstraction.Humans
manage complexity through abstraction. For example, people do not think of a car
as a set of tens of thousands of individual parts. They think of it as a well-defined
object with its own unique behavior.
• This abstraction allows people to use a car to drive to the grocery store without
being overwhelmed by the complexity of the individual parts.
• They can ignore the details of how the engine, transmission, and braking systems
work. Instead, they are free to utilize the object as a whole

Inheritance
• Inheritance is the process by which one object acquires the properties of another object. 
For example, a Golden Retriever is part of the classification dog, which in turn is part of 
the mammal class, which is under the larger class animal.
By use of inheritance, an object need only define those qualities that make it unique
within its class. It can inherit its general attributes from its parent. Thus, it is the
inheritance mechanism that makes it possible for one object to be a specific instance of a
more general case.
Most people naturally view the world as made up of objects

Polymorphism 
• Polymorphism (from Greek, meaning “many forms”) is a feature that allows one
interface to be used for a general class of actions. The specific action is
determined by the exact nature of the situation.
• Consider a stack (which is a last-in, first-out list). You might have a program that
requires three types of stacks. One stack is used for integer values, one for
floating-point values, and one for characters. The algorithm that implements
each stack is the same, even though the data being stored differs.

environment that supports the development of far more robust and scalable
programs than does the process-oriented model.
• A well-designed hierarchy of classes is the basis for reusing the code in which you
have invested time and effort developing and testing.
• Encapsulation allows you to migrate your implementations over time without
